title: Sentence Structure and Conjunctions
tagline: The functional grammar section in two halves: how a sentence is built, and the words that join its parts.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE English Language syllabus (Examination Year 2027 and 2028 documents as reproduced by Scribd, Oswal Publishers and Shaalaa; cisce.org returned 403). Every model text, question and answer is original practice; no board examination paper was consulted.

overview.intro: The functional grammar section of the ICSE Language paper names sentence structure and conjunctions among the areas to be tested, and both halves of this chapter are examinable in three different ways: as correction of faulty sentences, as transformation of one kind of sentence into another, and as fill-in work choosing the word that joins two clauses correctly. Sentence structure begins with the architecture — subject and predicate, phrase and clause, word order — and moves to the three shapes that matter: the simple sentence with a single independent clause, the compound sentence of two independent clauses properly joined, and the complex sentence of an independent clause with one or more dependants. Conjunctions are the joints: coordinating words that balance equals, subordinating words that rank a clause below another, correlative pairs that work in twos, and conjunctive adverbs that hinge whole sentences together. This chapter teaches each family with original examples, then the two skills the paper actually asks for — combining sentences without changing their meaning, and repairing fragments, run-ons and comma splices.

learningOutcomes: Analyse a sentence into subject, predicate, phrase and clause.
Distinguish simple, compound and complex sentences by their clause structure.
Classify conjunctions into their four families and use each correctly.
Combine sentences into compound and complex forms without altering meaning.
Diagnose and repair fragments, run-ons and comma splices.

learn.title: Before you read: grammar as architecture

blocks.text: Sentence structure is best approached as building rather than as rule-keeping. Every sentence is an answer to a question about a subject, and its worth is decided by whether the reader can see, at once, what is being said about what. Two units do all the work. The phrase is a group of words that functions as one unit but contains no subject-predicate pair of its own; the clause contains a subject and a predicate and can therefore stand as a sentence or be folded into a larger one. Once you can point at clauses, the three shapes of the sentence become obvious: one independent clause gives you the simple sentence, two properly joined give you the compound, and an independent clause carrying a dependent one gives you the complex. Conjunctions are then simply the mortar — and the examinable fact about them is that different mortars hold different loads: some join equals, some rank one clause below another, some work in pairs, and some hinge whole sentences. Prepare to work with a pencil in hand: this chapter’s questions all ask you to point, join or repair, and architecture is learned by rebuilding.

items: Phrase versus clause: only the clause has its own subject and predicate.
The three shapes: simple, compound, complex — count the clauses and their rank.
Conjunctions are joints with different load ratings.
The paper asks you to point, join or repair — practice must be active.

learn.title: Sentence anatomy: subject, predicate, phrase, clause

blocks.text: Start with the division every sentence can survive: subject and predicate. The subject is what the sentence is about — the person, thing or idea doing, suffering or being named; the predicate says something of it, built around the verb, with whatever the verb drags behind it. A sentence may have several subjects and predicates joined together and still be one sentence, provided the parts are properly connected. Inside that frame, distinguish the phrase from the clause without mercy. The phrase is a compact unit doing one job — a noun phrase filling a subject slot, a prepositional phrase adding place or time — but it never carries its own subject-predicate pair. The clause does: it is a little sentence with an ambition, either to stand alone as an independent clause or to lean on a bigger one as a dependent clause. That single distinction explains why sentences fail. A collection of phrases is a fragment; two independent clauses with nothing joining them is a run-on; and a dependent clause stranded without its head is an unfinished thought. The examination tests exactly these three failures, so practise locating subjects and predicates in sentences until the eye does it automatically.

learn.title: The three shapes: simple, compound, complex

blocks.text: The simple sentence holds one independent clause: whatever its length, it states one situation, even if subject and predicate are joined with several items. Its strength is directness; its danger, when overextended, is the series that loses its reader. The compound sentence sets two independent clauses side by side, joined by a coordinating conjunction with the correct punctuation — a comma before the joining word — so that the two situations are presented as equals of equal weight. The complex sentence introduces a dependency: a subordinator folds one clause beneath another, and the reader is told which idea governs which — cause before effect, condition before consequence, time around event. That ranking is what the complex sentence buys and what the compound cannot supply: relationship rather than mere addition. A compound-complex sentence, combining both, exists in the syllabus as awareness rather than as a target. The examination’s transformation work lives here: turning a pair of simple sentences into a compound says the two matter equally, while turning them into a complex says one explains the other — and the meaning of your answer changes with the choice, so the choice must be deliberate rather than decorative.

items: Simple: one independent clause; strength in directness, danger in overextension.
Compound: two independent clauses as equals, joined with a comma plus conjunction.
Complex: a dependent clause ranked under an independent one — cause, condition or time.
Transformation changes meaning: addition and explanation are different claims.
Compound-complex: known as awareness, not exercised as a target.

blocks.text: Conjunctions divide cleanly into four families, and each family has its own grammar. Coordinating conjunctions join grammatical equals — words, phrases or independent clauses — and the common ones are remembered by their letters: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. Between two independent clauses they take a comma before them, and each word carries its own logic: but and yet oppose, or offers alternatives, for gives a reason, so gives a result. Subordinating conjunctions — because, although, if, when, while, unless, until, whether, since, before, after — place one clause beneath another, and the clause they introduce becomes dependent: it may lead the sentence, but it cannot stand alone. Correlative conjunctions work in pairs: either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also, both … and, whether … or — and the rule that earns marks is that each half must balance the same kind of element, while the verb or noun closest to the second half often governs agreement, so that neither the manager nor the clerks are responsible follows the nearer subject. Conjunctive adverbs — however, therefore, moreover, nevertheless, otherwise, meanwhile — do not join clauses directly: they hinge sentences, and they need a semicolon or a full stop before them rather than a comma alone. Knowing which family a word belongs to tells you its punctuation as well as its meaning, which is half of what the paper asks.

blocks.text: Two practical skills close the chapter. Combination takes two or more sentences and rebuilds them as one, and the choice of target shape decides what the result means: a coordinating conjunction keeps the ideas level, while a subordinator makes one explain the other, so read the relationship first and pick the joint that expresses it — cause, contrast, condition or time. Replace rather than attach: when a subordinator joins two sentences, the original link-word between them usually has to go, or you will write because because. Repair is the opposite operation, and it targets three named faults. The fragment is a group of words with no subject, no predicate or a stranded clause, fixed by giving it the piece it lacks. The run-on fuses independent clauses with nothing between them, and the comma splice fuses them with only a comma — both are cured by proper joining: a comma plus coordinating conjunction, a semicolon between balanced clauses, or a conjunctive adverb with its own punctuation. The examination often hands you a faulty sentence and asks for the correction, which is why every fault should be practised from both directions — building up and taking apart.

learn.title: For the examination, and what to verify yourself

blocks.text: Three question types recycle this chapter. Identification: name the kind of sentence or the family of the conjunction — answer by clause count and rank, then by family, and you cannot go wrong. Transformation: combine or split sentences — always read the relationship first, then choose the joint, then check the punctuation. Correction: repair the fault named or implied — locate the missing subject, the run-on or the splice, and fix only what is faulty, because over-correcting a sentence that is partly right loses the mark you had. Fill-in questions test the conjunction that fits the logic: contrast calls for although or however, condition for if or unless, cause for because or since, and the choice between them is a matter of meaning, not of habit. The questions below exercise all four families in all three formats. Since this is functional grammar, work them on paper and check each answer against the rule rather than against your ear — the ear is trained by exactly these exercises.

items: Identification: clause count and rank first, family second.
Correction: fix only what is faulty.
Fill-in: choose by logic — contrast, condition, cause, time.
Check answers against the rule, not against habit.

keyPoints: A clause has its own subject and predicate; a phrase does not.
Independent clauses stand alone; dependent clauses are introduced by a subordinator.
Simple: one independent clause. Compound: two independent clauses joined properly. Complex: a dependent clause ranked under an independent one.
Transformation changes meaning: joining as equals claims addition; subordinating claims relationship.
Coordinating conjunctions — for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — join equals and take a comma before them between clauses.
Subordinating conjunctions — because, although, if, unless, when, until … — create dependence.
Correlative conjunctions work in pairs and must balance equal elements; agreement follows the nearer subject.
Conjunctive adverbs — however, therefore, moreover — hinge sentences and need a semicolon before them.
Fragments, run-ons and comma splices are the three faults the paper repairs.
Choose the joint by logic — cause, contrast, condition, time — then check the punctuation.
examFocus: “Name the kind of sentence” — count the clauses and rank them.
“Use a conjunction to join these sentences” — pick the family that expresses the relationship.
“Correct the following” — repair only the missing subject, run-on or splice.
“Fill in the blank with the correct conjunction” — decide the logic first, then the word.
“Combine into a complex sentence” — subordinator in, original link-word out, punctuation checked.

vocabulary.meaning: the part of a sentence that says something of the subject, built on the verb.
a group of words containing its own subject and predicate.
a clause able to stand alone as a complete sentence.
a clause introduced by a subordinator and unable to stand alone.
a joining word that links grammatical equals — for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
a word that ranks a clause beneath another — because, although, unless.

questions.prompt: Which of these groups contains only coordinating conjunctions?
questions.explanation: The coordinating family is for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so; the other options hold subordinators, correlatives and conjunctive adverbs respectively.
questions.commonMistake: Either and neither are correlative halves, not coordinators.

questions.prompt: A sentence built from one independent clause is called:
questions.explanation: Clause count and rank decide the shape: one independent clause is simple; two joined equals are compound; a dependent clause under an independent one is complex.
questions.commonMistake: Length is irrelevant — a long sentence with one clause is still simple.

questions.prompt: Which punctuation correctly joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction?
options: A comma after the conjunction only
questions.explanation: Between two independent clauses the pattern is comma plus coordinating conjunction; without the comma the result is a fused sentence.
questions.commonMistake: The comma goes before the joining word, not after it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a correlative pair?
options: Neither the manager nor the clerks were responsible.
Neither the manager nor the clerks was responsible.
Neither nor the manager the clerks were responsible.
The manager neither were responsible nor the clerks.
questions.answer: Neither the manager nor the clerks were responsible.
questions.explanation: Correlatives must balance equal elements, and the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it — clerks, plural, takes were.
questions.commonMistake: Agreement follows the nearer subject, not the first one named.

questions.prompt: Two independent clauses may also be linked by a conjunctive adverb such as ______, which needs a semicolon before it.
questions.explanation: Conjunctive adverbs — however, therefore, moreover, nevertheless — hinge whole sentences, so they take a semicolon before and a comma after.
questions.commonMistake: A comma alone before however creates a comma splice.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a phrase from a clause with one example of each.
questions.answer: A clause contains its own subject and predicate — for example, because the train was late — and can be independent or dependent. A phrase is a group of words functioning as one unit but with no subject–predicate pair — for example, at the far end of the platform. The test is simple: ask whether the unit has its own subject doing or being something.
questions.explanation: The distinction is defined by the subject–predicate test and illustrated with one of each.
questions.commonMistake: Do not define a clause as “a group of words”; that describes both units and marks nothing.

questions.prompt: State the three common faults in sentence structure and how each is repaired.
questions.answer: The fragment: words with no subject, no predicate, or a stranded dependent clause — repaired by supplying the missing element or attaching the clause to a complete sentence. The run-on: two independent clauses with nothing between them — repaired by proper joining with a comma plus conjunction, a semicolon, or a conjunctive adverb with its own punctuation. The comma splice: two independent clauses bridged by a comma alone — repaired in exactly the same way, by replacing the lone comma with a correct joint.
questions.explanation: All three faults are named with their definition and their repair, which is the complete answer.
questions.commonMistake: Run-on and comma splice are different faults — do not merge them.

questions.prompt: Combine into one complex sentence using a subordinator of concession: The rain was heavy. The match continued.
questions.answer: Although the rain was heavy, the match continued.
questions.explanation: Although expresses concession: the dependent clause is ranked under the independent one, and the original link between the two statements disappears with the rewrite.
questions.commonMistake: Writing Although it was raining heavy … — the subordinator takes a clause, not an adjective phrase, and heavy is an adverbial use here.

questions.prompt: Explain the four families of conjunctions, giving the punctuation rule that belongs to each.
questions.answer: Coordinating conjunctions — for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — join grammatical equals, up to two independent clauses, and between clauses they take a comma before the joining word: the comma belongs to the joint, not to the sentence’s start. Subordinating conjunctions — because, although, if, when, while, unless, until, whether, since, before, after — introduce a dependent clause and rank it beneath an independent one; the clause may lead the sentence, in which case a comma follows it, or follow it, in which case normally no comma is needed. Correlative conjunctions — either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also, both … and, whether … or — work in pairs, so each half must balance the same kind of element, and agreement is governed by the subject nearer the verb: neither the manager nor the clerks were. Conjunctive adverbs — however, therefore, moreover, nevertheless, otherwise — relate whole sentences rather than joining clauses, so they require a semicolon before them and a comma after: the sentence boundary must remain visible. Each family therefore carries its own punctuation, which is why identification of the family is half the marks in any correction question.
questions.explanation: The four families are named with members, function and the punctuation rule each carries — the full structure the question asks for.
questions.commonMistake: Do not give the families without their punctuation; the rule is the second half of the marks.

questions.prompt: “Combining sentences is a change of meaning, not merely of shape.” Discuss, with examples of your own.
questions.answer: The claim holds because every joint encodes a relationship, and the relationship is part of what the sentence says. Take two flat statements: the bell rang, and the children left the hall. Joined with and, they remain equals — a sequence, no explanation offered. Joined with so, the first becomes the cause of the second, and the writer now asserts a consequence the original pair only implied. Joined with before the children left, the time-relation is reversed and the bell is placed in the background. Each result reports the same two events, and each makes a different claim about them — addition, causation, temporal framing — so the meaning has moved with the shape. The same logic governs correction and subordination: turning a run-on into a semicolon join keeps the ideas level, while recasting one as a dependent clause subordinates it, and a writer who joins mechanically will say something he did not intend. A counter-argument should be weighed: sometimes one combination is forced by grammar — a contrast demands but or although, a condition demands if — leaving no free choice and therefore, arguably, no meaning shift. True, but the force of the general case survives it: wherever a genuine choice exists between coordinate and subordinate, the choice changes the emphasis, the causality or the timeline, and an examiner marks the relationship you have written. That is why combination questions are read for sense and not only for grammaticality: the correct answer is the one that means what the situation means.
questions.explanation: The essay demonstrates three combinations of one pair producing three claims, concedes the cases where grammar forces the joint, and grounds the general case in what examiners actually mark.
questions.commonMistake: Do not answer with rules alone; the discuss form needs worked examples of meaning shifting.
